tagline: College streets, a lost canal and the Harrison family’s Ohio home.
intro: Oxford is a college town along Four Mile Creek; farther south, Okeana sits on Dry Fork Creek. Near the southern end of the journey, Cleves lies between the Great Miami and Ohio rivers, with North Bend separating it from the Ohio.

The Cincinnati and Whitewater Canal opened in 1843, using a tunnel completed six years earlier beneath the ridge between North Bend and Cleves. William Henry Harrison supported the canal, sold land for its right-of-way and supplied timber and bricks for the tunnel. Flood damage brought abandonment in 1856; trains later used the tunnel from 1863 to 1888. It has since filled with silt almost to the ceiling.

Begin with Oxford’s Miami University, then Okeana on State Route 126 and Harrison, a former Whitewater Canal stop. At Cleves, North Bend lies immediately south; William Henry Harrison’s tomb is there on Brower Road. Finish at Elizabethtown, where U.S. 50 passes through the Great Miami River valley.

moments.title: Oxford
moments.text: Freedom Summer’s civil rights campaign began with orientations at Western College for Women in June 1964. The event is commemorated near Kumler Chapel on the Western campus, now part of Miami University. Western College operated from 1853 to 1974, first as a seminary and later as a liberal arts college. It merged with Miami in 1974.

moments.title: Harrison
moments.text: Harrison was named for William Henry Harrison when the town was laid out in 1810, before his presidency. It became one of the Whitewater Canal’s few Ohio stops. A different transport connection was broken on July 13, 1863, when Morgan’s Raiders, a Confederate cavalry force, passed through and burned the Whitewater River bridge near the town’s southwest side. The first train reached Harrison Township in 1864. The depot built in 1882 at West Broadway and Railroad Avenue later burned down. Across the state line is West Harrison, Indiana, separated from Harrison by State Street.

moments.title: William Henry Harrison Tomb
moments.text: William Henry Harrison’s burial at North Bend followed a first burial in Washington. He died on April 4, 1841, one month after taking office. His family chose the crest of Mt. Nebo on their estate, and he was interred there on July 7. His wife Anna and son John Scott are also buried at the memorial. John Scott links two presidencies: he was William Henry’s son and Benjamin Harrison’s father. In 1919, the Ohio General Assembly formally accepted the family’s bequest and funded care of the neglected tomb and grounds.
